doc.title: Milt Fillius interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 18, 2000

title: Selling the shipyard and leaving a conglomerate over phony financing
summary: He sold to Kaiser, returned to the banker's conglomerate, and quit on finding the tuna was pledged to three banks.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: But you went from there to a conglomerate that had a whole bunch of different things going on.
Did you move from those things because you needed a new challenge?

Well the shipyard we built into a big thing. It’s now the biggest shipyard on the west coast. And it was the biggest employer in San Diego at the time I left. We sold it to Kaiser Enterprises. And after a year and a half with Kaiser I decided I didn’t belong in © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-

that big operation. So I told my good friend Edgar Kaiser I was going to leave, and did. And I went back with the guy who owned the shipyard in the first place, who now had a bank and a cannery and a bunch of tuna boats and the Yellow Cab Company in L.A. and San Francisco and a bus line in Kansas City. So I became the Executive Vice President of that company and ran all those businesses. And I was doing all right I guess. Then I discovered that there was some phony financing going on. I was on the board incidentally of this company. And I discovered that my boss the banker was playing games. And for example I had several million dollars worth of tuna sitting in the warehouse, canned tuna, and found it was hocked to three separate banks. So I said we can’t do that, you can’t do that. He said oh yes I can. I said well okay. But not with me you can’t. So I left. It was just that I didn’t want to be part of it. Several years later it collapsed. And too bad. Because he was a nice guy. But he just didn’t understand that the law was made for him. And he and Dick Nixon were friends and you know, they thought alike.
